list.listitem: Primary prevention with tetanus immunization is key to prevention of disease. C

Diagnosis is made on the basis of acute onset general muscle spasm or trismus (lockjaw), especially in patients with a recent high-risk wound or in those who have never received a primary tetanus immunization series. C

Treatment consists of debridement of the wound, antibiotic treatment with penicillin or metronidazole to eradicate the organism, B and immunoglobulin therapy to bind the toxin if the patient is not appropriately immunized. C
Patients will require supportive care, C which may include ventilatory support, magnesium for autonomic instability, and labetalol to treat hypertension and tachycardia. B

background.definition: Tetanus is an acute, often fatal disease caused by a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani. Tetanus infection usually presents with trismus, followed by generalized rigidity. Glottic spasm, impaired respiratory function, respiratory failure, and autonomic instability can result in death. Tetanus can be prevented by vaccination of children and adults.

list.listitem: A total of 14,529 cases were reported worldwide in 2006, though this number is likely an underestimate.
There were 213,000 estimated deaths worldwide in 2002, with most of these deaths occurring in children younger than 5 years.
Total tetanus rates in selected international regions: sub-Saharan Africa: 15/100,000; India: 40 to 60/100,000.
Worldwide in 2007: Neonatal tetanus incidence (reported cases) is highest in China, India, and Pakistan; total tetanus is highest in Congo, Ghana, Uganda, Bangladesh, India, and Philippines.

In the United States, widespread vaccination has caused the incidence to decline from 3.9 cases per million in 1947 to 0.16 cases per million (1998-2000). Older adults have a higher burden of tetanus, likely due to the lack of primary vaccination series in childhood.
Neonatal tetanus in the United States is rare, with only 3 cases reported during 1990 to 2004 (CDC unpublished data, 2005).

Tetanus is caused by spores from the bacteria Clostridium tetani, which live throughout the environment and enter the body through broken skin. C. tetani spores germinate into Gram-positive bacilli. These bacteria thrive in oxygen-poor sites, such as necrotic tissue from blunt trauma and deep puncture wounds.
Tetanus is not passed from person-to-person.

Neonatal tetanus can occur extremely rarely in newborns who are exposed to C. tetani prior to immunization and whose mothers do not have enough circulating antibodies to protect the infant by transplacental transfer. Entry is through the umbilical stump, and risks include using nonsterile instruments to cut the umbilical cord and the application of animal dung to the cord (a common birth practice in some cultures).

Tetani bacilli produce the endotoxin tetanospasmin, a strong neurotoxin that causes muscle contraction. It is produced by the bacteria at the site of inoculation and then travels by the bloodstream to the central nervous system (CNS). It works directly on CNS neurons to cause decreased release of GABA (glycine and gamma-aminobutyric acid), resulting in disinhibition of spinal reflex arcs. This causes multiple, intense muscle spasms.
Tetanospasmin also disrupts presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing autonomic dysfunction by inhibiting sympathetic reflexes at the spinal level.
Symptoms usually occur within 7 days of the injury or exposure and lasts up to 4 weeks or longer. It is usually followed by a prolonged convalescence.
The diptheria toxoid, tetanus toxid and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine is recommended at ages 2, 4, and 6 months with a 4th dose between 15 to 18 months, and a booster at 4 to 6 years. (5 total)

The tetanus toxoid, reduced diptheria toxoid and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine is recommended between 11 to 18 years for one dose as well as during each pregnancy between 27 to 36 weeks gestation.
The tetanus and diptheria toxid (Td) vaccine is recommended for 1 dose every 10 years.

A 3-dose primary series of tetanus toxoid given in infancy (typically at 2, 4, and 6 months) with a booster at 5 to 6 years of age is almost 100% effective for 5 to 10 years. AICP guidelines add a dose between 15 to 18 months as well for 5 total.

In the United States, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends adults receive a booster dose of tetanus toxoid every 10 years, or earlier as indicated for wound care. One booster in adolescents and adults, between the ages of 11 and 64 years, should also contain pertussis (Tdap).

In the United Kingdom, The National Health Service recommends a similar primary series of tetanus immunization starting after birth, with a final booster in adolescence. As long as an adult has had a total of 5 doses, further routine boosters are not recommended in adulthood unless a serious injury occurs.

In 2 large cohort studies, adverse reactions following vaccination were uncommon; the medically-attended local reaction rate was 3.6/10,000 following Td administration to adolescents and young adults and the relative risk for serious reactions in adults was 4 to 5 for Guillain-Barré syndrome and 1.5 to 2.0 for encephalopathy-encephalitis-meningitis, paralytic syndromes, seizures, and cranial nerve disorders, with similar results regardless of whether Td or Tdap was administered.

Fever less than or equal to 105F, fussiness, drowsiness, seizures within 3 days of a prior dose, and inconsolible crying for greater than 3 hours after a previous administration are not contraindications for recvieing another dose of DTaP or Tdap.

In 1 study, asking a patient whether they had a tetanus booster in the last 10 years is sensitive (92.4%; 95% CI, 89.0-95.0) but not specific (26.5%; 95% CI, 12.9-44.4) using the medical record as gold standard.
Using a longer needle (25 mm compared with 16 mm) for many of the combined tetanus immunizations is associated with few complications.
Tetanus infection does not confer immunity. Patients who have recovered from tetanus infection should receive the primary vaccination series.
Patients with tetanus-prone wounds should receive tetanus immunization and possibly immunoglobulin. See Drug Therapy section.
Tetanus infection is a clinical diagnosis. There are no useful diagnostic tests. C

Consider tetanus infection in any patient with generalized muscle spasm or trismus. In populations with a higher risk of tetanus (IV drug users, the elderly), the diagnosis may be considered earlier. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Physical examination reveals peritonsillar or odontogenic infection
Responds well to diphenhydramine or benztropine; absence of tonic contractions between spasms
Exposure to neuroleptic, fever, and altered mental status
Absence of trismus, responds to diazepam

list.listitem: Tetani will not grow in healthy tissue. A tetanus-prone wound is any wound that is: more than 6 hours old, more than 1 cm deep, grossly contaminated with dirt or debris, stellate in appearance, denervated or ischemic, or obviously infected. A retrospective review in Thailand found that 81% had a history of a wound or injury, with a mean age of 45 years.

Generalized tetanus is the most common type. Early symptoms include neck stiffness, sore throat, and difficulty opening the mouth. Later symptoms include lockjaw (masseter muscle spasm), risus sardonicus or "laugh of the clown" (facial muscle spasm), opisthotonus (tonic contractions that produce postures similar to decorticate posturing), respiratory failure, autonomic instability (arrhythmias, hyper/hypothermia, labile hypertension), rigid abdomen, apnea, and dysphagia.
Localized tetanus: a rare variation in which muscle spasm occurs only near the site of injury.
Cephalic tetanus: cranial nerve involvement only, though it usually progresses to full tetanus syndrome.
Neonatal tetanus: poor feeding and general irritability, progress to full body spasms and respiratory failure; usually presents within 14 days of birth.
There are no laboratory findings characteristic of tetanus; patients suspected of having tetanus should be treated without performing laboratory testing.
Culture of infected wounds may be performed but frequently fails to detect C. tetani.

Antibody concentrations should not be performed because negligible antibody levels are suggestive of, but not diagnostic for, tetanus. There is no convincing evidence of a protective level of antibody; the minimum tetanus antibody concentration has not been convincingly established. Fatalities have occurred in patients with tetanus antibody levels above what is often considered to be "protective."
Consider tetanus in any patient presenting with generalized muscle spasms, particularly if they have had a recent tetanus-prone wound.
Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis. Tissue culture is often negative and serological testing is not helpful.
Also consider tetanus infection in IV drug users, immunocompromised patients, and those who have never received the primary series of tetanus vaccines.
Debride wound and treat with either penicillin or metronidazole. B
Give human tetanus immunoglobulin (HTIG); if unavailable, use equine antitoxin. C
Supportive care should include ventilatory support, caloric support, and thromboembolism prophylaxis. C
Treat autonomic instability with magnesium sulfate. Labetalol can be used to treat hypertension and tachycardia. B
Diazepam is commonly used for controlling muscle spasms but does not have good evidence of benefit. B
The goals of treatment are to (1) halt toxin production, (2) neutralize unbound toxin, and (3) control symptoms and provide supportive care.

Once the disease is acquired, treatment consists of administration of immunoglobulins. Antitetanus serum (equine) or tetanus immunoglobulin (human) can help avoid death. These can be used intramuscularly or intrathecally. A meta-analysis of 12 studies with 942 patients found reduced mortality for intrathecal administration (RR 0.71; 95% CI, 0.62-0.81) in the treatment of tetanus, especially for adults and when a higher dose (>250 units) is used.

Toxin production is halted through wound debridement and antibiotic treatment with either benzyl penicillin G 2 million to 10 million units daily, benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units intramuscularly, or metronidazole 600 mg every 6 hours for 10 days.

Unbound toxin is neutralized through passive immunity with HTIG. The dose is 3000 to 6000 units intramuscularly or 5000 to 10,000 units IV. In countries without HTIG, equine antitoxin 1500 to 3000 units either intramuscularly or IV is used.

Magnesium sulfate may reduce autonomic instability. It is given as a loading dose of 40 mg per kg infused more than 30 minutes, followed by a continuous infusion of 2 g per hour (for patients who weigh more than 45 kg) or 1.5 kg per hour (for patients lighter than 45 kg). Labetalol is also used for the treatment of autonomic signs such as hypertension and tachycardia.

Diazepam has not been evaluated properly for the treatment of tetanus. However, it is frequently used at IV doses of 10 to 30 mg to control spasms and for sedation. Pancuronium may increase autonomic instability and should be avoided. Intrathecal baclofen, 500 mcg (if patient weighs less than 55 kg) and 1000 mcg (if heavier than 55 kg), has been shown to be effective in case reports.
See CDC Guidelines for tetanus wound prophylaxis.
Suspected tetanus-infected wounds should be debrided to halt production of the toxin.
Vitamin C may reduce mortality from tetanus infection. However, only 1 poorly reported trial of IV vitamin C (1 g/day) in 117 patients in Bangladesh supports this finding.
Supportive care should include ventilatory support, caloric support, and thromboembolism prophylaxis.

In a small case series of five patients with tetanus, the administration of intrathecal immunoglobulin for the treatment of tetanus was not associated with serious adverse effects. All 5 returned to work within 240 days of hospital discharge.
There is a high case fatality rate, especially if hospital facilities do not have ventilatory support. C
The mortality rate in the United States during 1998 to 2000 was 18%.

In a 25-year Thai case series of 47 patients with tetanus, 80.8% had a history of a wound and clinical severity was associated with older than 60 years, puncture wound, onset time of less than 7 days, and generalized tetanus (91.4% of cases); only 2 patients died.

In the United States, older adults have a higher burden of tetanus disease. This may be due to waning immunity or to the high proportion of elderly people who never received a primary series of immunizations as children. A serological survey in the United States from 1988 to 1994 demonstrated only 31% of adults older than 70 years had fully protective antibody levels to tetanus.
Pregnancy is not a contraindication for the Tdap vaccine.

The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends that pregnant women (1) receive Tdap during each pregnancy, irrespective of the patient's prior history of receiving Tdap, between 27 and 36 weeks gestation for maximal maternal antibody response (although tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy). If Tdap was not administered during pregnancy it should be given in the immediate postpartum period before discharge from the hospital.

Preterm infants who have been given steroids for chronic lung disease may have a suppressed antibody response to diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccines. However, it is unclear whether this is clinically important.
Premature children should receive the vaccination on the normal chronological schedule.

Children under 7 who have not had the recommended vaccination schedule can catch up on vaccines by using 4 week intervals between doses 1, 2, and 3. Dose 4 should be given 6 months after dose 3. Dose 5 should be given between 4 to 6 years of age and at least 6 months after the 4th dose. All doses are of the DTaP Vaccine.

Children 7 years through 18 years of age catch up depending on how many doses they have recieved in the past and when they recieved them. Refer to the CDC guidlines for specific pathways. Only 1 dose of the catch up series is TDaP. All remainding doses are Td.
